Priya has 2 phones? Kabir has none? Every row must fit the same columns — so you get NULLs or a brand-new table.
Fixed schema

JOINs everywhere

MongoDB Series · Lecture 01
Scalability · watch it move
Bigger machine, or more machines?
MongoDB was designed to scale out: add ordinary servers and let the data spread across them.
MongoDB Series · Lecture 01 · Animation is illustrative; sizes are examples
Tool 1 · Replica set = copies for safety
If one server dies, another takes over
1 · Primary
Takes every write from the app.
2 · Secondaries
Copy each change from the primary's oplog (operation log).
3 · Failover
Primary silent? The others vote a new primary, automatically.
MongoDB Series · Lecture 01 · White dot = write · Amber dot = copied change
Tool 2 · Sharding = split the data
Too big for one server? Slice it.
Shard key
A field you choose (here: name) decides which shard a document lives on.
mongos router
The app talks to one router; it sends each query to the right shard.
Config servers
Keep the map: which key range is on which shard.
MongoDB Series · Lecture 01 · In production, each shard is itself a replica set
The CAP theorem · every distributed DB's trade-off
When the network splits, pick C or A
C
A
P
Consistency everyone reads the latest data
MongoDB's default sits on the C–P edge
Availability · always answers
Partition tolerance
P is not optional. Networks fail, so a distributed database must survive splits.
MongoDB favours C. Writes go to one primary; during an election, writes pause for a moment rather than disagree.
…but it's tunable. Read/write concern and read preference let you trade safety for speed.
MongoDB Series · Lecture 01 · Cassandra, by contrast, leans toward A
System design view · What is I/O?
I/O = moving data in and out
Input/Output is any trip data takes between the CPU and memory, disk or network. Each trip has a very different cost:
Where the data is
Time (log scale)
Real
If RAM = 1 sec
RAM (memory)
~100 ns
1 second
SSD read
~100 µs
~17 minutes
Hard-disk seek
~10 ms
~1 day
India ↔ US trip
~200 ms
~23 days
A fast database is one that avoids disk and network trips. That's the whole game.
MongoDB Series · Lecture 01 · Rough, commonly quoted latency figures; real hardware varies
Inside a write · insertOne()
How MongoDB writes fast and stays safe
1 · Write to RAM
The change lands in the WiredTiger cache in memory — fast.
2 · Append to journal
A sequential log on disk, so a crash can be replayed.
3 · Checkpoint
About every 60 s, changed pages are flushed to data files.
MongoDB Series · Lecture 01 · Animation sped up · WiredTiger is MongoDB's default storage engine
Inside a read · find()
Search every page, or use the index?
COLLSCAN
No index
Checks every document to find the match. Slow when you have millions.
IXSCAN
With an index
Jumps root → branch → leaf → document in a few hops, like a book's index.
Bonus speed-up: if the pages it needs are already in RAM (the cache), there's no disk I/O at all. Indexes get their own lecture later.

Level 1 · Database commands
Find, enter and remove a database
show dbs
View all databases on the server.
use dbName
Switch to a database — or create it (it appears once it holds data).
db
Which database am I in right now?
db.dropDatabase()
Deletes the current database. No undo — double-check with db first.
mongosh
test> show dbs admin   40.00 KiB config  72.00 KiB local   80.00 KiB test> use college switched to db college college> db college
MongoDB Series · Lecture 01 · Sizes shown are sample output
Level 2 · Collection commands
List, create and drop collections
show collections
List the collections in the current database.
db.createCollection('comments')
Create a collection named comments.
db.comments.drop()
Deletes the collection and every document in it.
Shortcut: inserting into a collection that doesn't exist creates it automatically.
mongosh
college> db.createCollection(   'comments') { ok: 1 } college> show collections comments college> db.comments.drop() true

Level 3 · Documents · C for Create
Insert one, or insert many
db.comments.insertOne({   'name': 'MERN',   'lang': 'JavaScript',   'member_since': 5 })
insertOne( {…} )
Pass one object. MongoDB replies with the new _id:
insertedId: ObjectId('…')
db.comments.insertMany([   { name: 'jklu', lang: 'JavaScript', member_since: 5 },   { name: 'manipal', lang: 'Python', member_since: 3 },   { name: 'JDKPoint', lang: 'Java', member_since: 4 } ])
insertMany( [ … ] )
Pass an array of objects — square brackets! One trip to the server for all three.
MongoDB Series · Lecture 01 · Quotes around keys are optional in mongosh
R for Read
Reading documents back
db.comments.find()
Show all documents in the collection.
db.comments.find().pretty()
Same, nicely formatted (mongosh does this by default).
db.comments.findOne({name: 'MERN'})
Only the first document that matches.
db.comments.find({lang:'Python'})
Search with a filter — next slide shows how.
db.comments.find().limit(2)
Return at most 2 documents.
db.comments.find().count()
How many? Modern form: countDocuments({}).
college> db.comments.findOne({name: 'MERN'}) { _id: ObjectId('…'), name: 'MERN', lang: 'JavaScript', member_since: 5 }
MongoDB Series · Lecture 01 · count() on a cursor is deprecated in new versions; it still works with a warning
Searching · how a filter works
The filter is a "shape" to match
db.comments.find({ lang: 'Python' })
name: 'MERN' lang: 'JavaScript'
name: 'jklu' lang: 'JavaScript'
name: 'manipal' lang: 'Python' ✓
name: 'JDKPoint' lang: 'Java'
{ lang: 'Python' }
keeps only documents where lang equals 'Python'
Result · 1 document
{ name: 'manipal',   lang: 'Python',   member_since: 3 }
MongoDB Series · Lecture 01 · Two fields in one filter = both must match (AND)

Less than, greater than: $lt, $gt…

Sorting results
1 means up, −1 means down
db.comments.find().sort({ member_since: -1 }).pretty()
{ member_since: 1 } · ascending
manipal
3
JDKPoint
4
MERN
5
jklu
5
{ member_since: -1 } · descending
MERN
5
jklu
5
JDKPoint
4
manipal
3
Chain them like LEGO: find( filter ) → sort( order ) → limit( n ) — e.g. the top 2 longest members.
MongoDB Series · Lecture 01 · Ties (two 5s) keep no guaranteed order unless you add a second sort field
U for Update · $set and upsert
An update has three parts
db.comments.updateOne({name: 'Microsoft NOIDA'},   {$set: {'name': 'jklu', 'lang': 'JavaScript', 'member_since': 51}},   {upsert: true})
① Filter — which document?
② Update — $set these fields
③ Options — upsert = update or insert
Does any document have name 'Microsoft NOIDA'?
Yes → change only the fields inside $set.
No → (our case!) upsert creates a brand-new document: jklu · JavaScript · 51.
MongoDB Series · Lecture 01 · Without upsert: true, no match simply means nothing changes
More update operators
Add to a number. Rename a field.
$inc · increment
db.comments.update({name: 'Google'},   {$inc: { member_since: 2 }})
BEFORE
name: 'Google' member_since: 5
AFTER
name: 'Google' member_since: 7
$rename · rename a field
db.comments.update({name: 'Facebook'},   {$rename: { member_since: 'member' }})
BEFORE
name: 'Facebook' member_since: 3
AFTER
name: 'Facebook' member: 3
Modern mongosh: update() is deprecated — write updateOne() or updateMany() instead. Same operators.
MongoDB Series · Lecture 01 · Example values: insert 'Google' and 'Facebook' documents first to try these
D for Delete
Know your blast radius
db.comments.deleteOne({ name: 'Google' })  // removes the first match
deleteOne()
1 document
deleteMany()
every match · {} = all docs
.drop()
the whole collection
dropDatabase()
everything in the database
MongoDB Series · Lecture 01 · Bar height = how much you lose · There is no undo button
